There are two ways to detect a secret, and they are different enough that a good scanner uses both and a bad one pretends one is enough. The first is the pattern rule: a regex that matches the known shape of a known credential. The cloud provider key starts with a specific prefix. The git token has a specific format. articles.author: Surya Kanth
articles.description:
PART 1: ARCHITECTURAL OVERVIEW



  
  
  1.1 Primitive vs Reference Types


Primitives are immutable, fixed-size (or engine-optimized) values stored directly where the variable binding lives — conceptually the stack (execution context's variable environment). Objects are mutable, variable-size structures stored on the heap; the variable binding holds a pointer to that heap location.
This is NOT pass-by-reference in the C++/Pascal sense. JS is strictly call-by-value, but for objects, the value being copied is the reference itself — this hybrid model is called call-by-sharing.
function mutate(obj) { obj.x = 99; }      // mutates shared heap object
function reassign(obj) { obj = { x: 0 }; } // rebinds LOCAL copy of pointer only

let o = { x: 1 };
mutate(o);    console.log(o.x); // 99 — heap …
articles.title: JavaScript Data Types

articles.author: ke jia
articles.description:
The question of where to run the secret scan has two popular answers, and both are right, and the teams that argue about it are arguing about the wrong thing. The pre-commit hook is the fast layer: it runs on your machine, in the moment, before the push, and it catches the leak at the point where the person who made the mistake is still at the keyboard and can fix it in thirty seconds. The CI scan is the enforcement layer: it runs on the server, on every push from every developer, including the ones who never set up a local hook, and it is the layer that cannot be skipped, bypassed, or forgotten. The argument is which one to have; the answer is which one is missing.
A comparison is a set of questions with two answers each, and the questions below are the ones the choice actually turns on, …
articles.title: Secret Scanning in CI vs in the Pre-Commit Hook: Which Layer Should Catch It?

articles.description:
Rotating a leaked credential is the step everyone performs and almost nobody verifies, which is how the old key keeps working from a forgotten config file while the new one does the job. The re-scan is the verification, and it is a two-minute ritual that closes the loop: the scan found the value, the value was rotated, and now the scan confirms the old value is gone from the working tree. If it is still there, the rotation was only half done, and the second scan is the proof that the first one was not. The report format makes the comparison concrete: the same command before and after, the findings diffed against each other, and the old value either present or not.
